sm: This morning news show opens with a Nashville toy drive for the Metro Police Christmas Charities annual basket giveaway, now in its sixty-fifth year. Captain Keeler, this year's chief elf, says new unwrapped toys and money for food are being collected, and on Christmas Eve morning officers will deliver to over four hundred homes and more than a thousand children. Families are identified by officers and counselors who see a need. The hosts then note thirteen days until Thanksgiving and forty-two until Christmas, replay a 1997 story on the naming of the Nashville Predators, and show a tour of the new Nissan Stadium, whose roof is now fully enclosed on a two point two billion dollar project.

Stadium officials say more than ten thousand workers have logged over nine million hours, the project is on schedule, and the Titans get the keys on February 17th. The stadium has landed Super Bowl 64 in 2030, and the first big event should be a major concert in mid to late April. The weather forecast calls for a high of 49, the coldest day since March, with lows near 31 tonight and widespread frost this weekend. Other items include an adoptable dog named Almond, a nine inch Reese's peanut butter cup pie priced at fifty dollars, and a report that eighty-two percent of parents of young children have thought about saving for a future down payment.

The hosts discuss housing costs and down payment funds, then a Netherlands study finding that nearly a quarter of young adults pretend to be better off financially than they are. Forty-one percent struggle to admit they cannot afford something, and nearly thirty percent would rather suffer in silence than talk about money with family. Top stories follow. Microsoft reports encouraging recovery after a global outage hit Microsoft 365 services such as Outlook and Teams, and it says it does not believe a cyber attack was the cause. Senator Mark Pody of Lebanon is interested in an underground tunnel to ease traffic, and developer Simon broke ground on Sage Field, a one hundred acre shopping and dining development in Thompson's Station with about eighty shops. The Stuff the Truck toy drive is now collecting.

Organizer Carly Susson says the eighth annual Stuff the Truck is on December fourth at Topgolf, from five to ten in the evening, with the Spazmatics, an eighties and nineties cover band, and a DJ. The goal is fifteen hundred toys. Guests who bring a toy get a dinner ticket, and entry without one is thirty dollars. Last year they reached about 1,288 toys, and attendance grew from fifty to over 250. Also noted, 70 percent of viewers say they have started holiday shopping. A report from Blackman High School describes a reality fair where students manage budgets and a student-run credit union branch. The show closes with holiday budgeting tips from an Intuit QuickBooks report that found 63 percent of shoppers worry about higher prices.
